title: Intelligent agents
subtitle: Forget “thinking machines”: an agent senses, decides and acts. Everything in AI is a way of making that decision better.

sections.title: What is AI?
sections.body: AI has been defined four ways: systems that think like humans, act like humans (the Turing test), think rationally (logic) or act rationally. The last is the working definition: a rational agent does whatever is expected to maximise its performance measure given what it has perceived. Roots: philosophy, mathematics, psychology, neuroscience, linguistics and computer engineering; the field was named in 1956 (Dartmouth).

questions.prompt: The Turing test checks whether a machine can…

choices.text: Converse so well that a human judge cannot tell it from a person.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is a test of acting humanly.

sections.title: Agents and environments
sections.body: An agent perceives its environment through sensors and acts on it through actuators; its behaviour is a mapping from the percept history to an action. A thermostat, a robot vacuum and a chess program all fit.

choices.text: Change the environment, which produces new percepts.

sections.title: Kinds of agent
sections.body: Simple reflex: condition–action rules on the current percept (“if the floor is dirty, suck”). Model-based reflex: keeps internal state about what it cannot see. Goal-based: chooses actions that reach a goal (needs search and planning). Utility-based: maximises a measure of how good outcomes are, handling trade-offs. Learning agents improve from experience with a critic and a learning element.

questions.prompt: When do you need a utility-based rather than goal-based agent?

choices.text: When there are several ways to reach the goal and some are better (faster, safer, cheaper).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Utility ranks outcomes; a goal only says done or not.

sections.title: Properties of environments
sections.body: Fully vs partially observable; deterministic vs stochastic; episodic vs sequential; static vs dynamic; discrete vs continuous; single vs multi-agent. Chess is fully observable, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete, two-agent. Driving is partially observable, stochastic, dynamic and continuous — much harder.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The agent’s percepts do not reveal the full state.

problems.prompt: Classify a game of poker on observability and determinism.
problems.answer: Partially observable (other hands are hidden) and stochastic (the deal is random); also multi-agent and discrete.

sections.title: Agentic AI
sections.body: Modern language-model “agents” use the same loop: perceive (read a goal, tool outputs), decide (plan a step), act (call a tool, run code) and observe again. The classic vocabulary applies: what is the performance measure, what is observable, what happens when the model's world model is wrong?

questions.prompt: A language-model agent calling a search tool is performing the role of…

choices.text: An actuator acting on its environment.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The results come back as new percepts.

sections.title: Knowledge and learning
sections.body: Intelligence needs knowledge (facts and rules, represented so a program can use them) and the ability to learn it. Symbolic AI encodes knowledge by hand; machine learning extracts it from data. The two are combined in modern systems. The rest of the course is this split: search and logic, then learning.

worked.why: An expert system has 500 hand-written rules; a neural network has 10⁶ weights learned from examples.
Rules are inspectable but laborious; learned weights are cheap to acquire but hard to explain.

choices.text: Explicit rules and facts written by people.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: In contrast to weights learned from data.
